answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1937–2026 · college football coach; Notre Dame national champion, 1988
answer.sourceLine: This is the Holtz line people quote first, and nothing we found argues against him. What is missing is a record. Wikiquote ↗ puts it in its Attributed section with a single second-hand citation, and a phrase search across all of Wikiquote returns no other page carrying it — so there is no rival claimant, just an absence of evidence. We could not establish which team, which season, or which occasion.

source.excerpt: On this team, we’re all united in a common goal: to keep my job.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ files this line under Attributed, which is its own signal: the page has no sourced section at all, and every quotation on it carries the same kind of second-hand citation.

That citation is a Bleacher Report listicle, “Top 15 Funniest Lou Holtz Quotes” by Ben Weiximann. We could not retrieve it — the host is unreachable from our network — so we can neither confirm what it says nor what it cites. We are not counting it as corroboration.

A phrase search across the whole of English Wikiquote returns only the Lou Holtz page for this sentence. That is a meaningful negative in one direction — no one else is claiming it — and no help in the other, because an uncontested attribution is still an unsourced one.

Holtz’s own books would be the obvious place to look. The Internet Archive holds Winning Every Day (1998) ↗ and Wins, Losses, and Lessons (2006) ↗, but both are lending-restricted and cannot be searched full-text, so this line is neither confirmed nor ruled out there.
Quote Investigator has not examined this quotation, so there is no specialist finding to defer to.
source.excerptNote: The line as Wikiquote ↗ records it. Holtz held seven head-coaching jobs between 1969 and 2004; nothing we found ties the joke to any one of them.
source.rightsNote: We cannot name a first publication for this line, so we cannot point you at a document. What we can say is that it is not in the public domain: Holtz’s coaching and broadcasting career ran from 1969 to 2015, and everything published in the United States from 1931 onward is still under copyright protection. Treat it as in copyright and quote it as a quotation, with attribution, rather than reusing it as free text.

author.heading: About Lou Holtz
author.metaLine: 1937–2026 · American college football coach · Notre Dame, 1986–1996
author.bio: Lou Holtz (6 January 1937 – 4 March 2026) coached at six colleges and one NFL team across nearly three decades, most famously taking Notre Dame to an undefeated 1988 season and the national title. He finished with 249 college wins, spent a decade as an ESPN analyst after retiring from the sideline, and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2020. He was as well known for the one-liners as for the coaching — which is exactly why lines attached to his name need checking.

context.heading: The joke that fit the man
lead: Holtz took over programmes that were losing and made a running gag of his own precariousness. He coached at seven places between 1969 and 2004, including a single season with the New York Jets ↗ that he did not finish, so the joke had a factual spine under it.
It is the kind of line a coach reuses for twenty years in front of boosters and reporters, which is precisely why no one wrote down the first time.
